content: Oregano, also known as Pot Marjoram (Origanum vulgare), is a species of the Origanum genus. It is native to Europe, the Mediterranean region, and parts of southern and central Asia. This plant is a perennial herb that typically grows to a height of 20–80 cm. Its leaves are arranged oppositely and measure 1–4 cm in length. The flowers are purple, measuring 3–4 mm in length, and are produced in upright spikes. The name oregano originates from the Greek word origanon, which combines oros (meaning mountain) and ganousthai (meaning to delight in). Cultivation and Uses The subspecies Origanum vulgare hirtum is a significant culinary herb, particularly prominent in Greek and Italian cuisines. The leaves are the part of the plant used in cooking, and the dried form of oregano is often more flavorful than the fresh. Oregano is commonly incorporated into tomato sauces, fried vegetables, and grilled meats. Alongside basil, it plays a crucial role in defining the distinctive flavor profile of many Italian dishes. It pairs well with pickled olives, capers, and lovage leaves. Unlike most Italian herbs, oregano complements hot and spicy dishes, which are popular in southern Italy. In Greek cuisine, oregano is an essential ingredient. It enhances the flavor of Greek salads and is often used either on its own or as part of a lemon-olive oil sauce that accompanies nearly all fish, meat barbecues, and some casseroles. Oregano has an aromatic, warm, and slightly bitter taste, with its intensity varying depending on the quality. High-quality oregano can be so potent that it almost numbs the tongue, whereas cultivars adapted to colder climates often have a less satisfactory flavor. The composition of oregano's essential oil is significantly influenced by factors such as climate, season, and soil, more so than by differences between species. Related species, such as Origanum onites (native to Greece and Asia Minor) and Origanum heracleoticum (found in Italy, the Balkan Peninsula, and West Asia), share similar flavors. Marjoram, a closely related plant from Asia Minor, differs significantly in taste due to the absence of phenolic compounds in its essential oil. Some hybrid breeds exhibit a flavor profile that is intermediate between oregano and marjoram. The dish most commonly associated with oregano is pizza, and its relatives have likely been consumed in southern Italy for centuries. Health Benefits Oregano is rich in antioxidant activity, primarily due to its high content of phenolic acids and flavonoids. Studies (PMID 16218659, PMID 12730411) have demonstrated its antimicrobial properties, particularly against foodborne pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes. These characteristics make oregano potentially beneficial for both health and food preservation. In the Philippines, oregano (Coleus aromaticus) is not typically used for culinary purposes but is instead regarded as a medicinal plant. It is commonly employed to alleviate children's coughs. Other Plants Called Oregano Mexican oregano (Lippia graveolens), which belongs to the Verbenaceae family, is closely related to lemon verbena. This herb has been extensively studied for its potential medicinal uses and is commonly utilized in curandera (female shamanic) practices in Mexico and the southwestern United States. Mexican oregano has a flavor profile very similar to that of traditional oregano but is generally stronger. It is becoming increasingly available outside of Mexico, particularly in the United States. It is sometimes used as a substitute for epazote leaves, although the reverse substitution is not effective. Several other plants are also referred to as oregano in various parts of Mexico, including Poliomintha longiflora, Lippia berlandieri, and Plectranthus amboinicus (syn. Coleus aromaticus), which is also known as Cuban oregano.
